items.titel: Machine learning-based prediction of critical load events in airborne wind energy systems
items.samenvatting_bron: Abstract. Predicting and avoiding critical load events is crucial for the reliable autonomous operation of airborne wind energy (AWE) systems. Such events can lead to actuator saturation, loss of steering authority, and increased structural stresses, eventually resulting in long-term degradation of the kite, tether, and ground-station components. The present study explores a data-driven approach to predicting tether force peaks, defined as instances in which the force exceeds a threshold set by the winch controller. The method is developed using a large-scale SCADA dataset from Kitepower's leading-edge inflatable V9 kite, including more than 1000 pumping cycles spanning 26 h of kite operation and covering a wide range of wind and operating conditions. Tether force peaks are detected and used to extract pre-peak time windows that capture the system behavior before each threshold exceedance. From these windows, statistical, temporal, and spectral features are computed from multiple kite, tether, and ground-station measurements. A supervised classification model is trained to distinguish normal operation from pre-peak dynamics. The proposed approach predicts critical load events 1 s in advance and shows strong generalization capability on flight data that was not used for training the model, correctly identifying 85.4 % of the critical load events (recall) and achieving a 90.9 % F1-score, a metric that indicates a strong balance between correctly detected events and false alarms

items.titel: From fragmented knowledge to scalable wetland restoration in Europe: The Restore4Life Integrated Wetland Reconstruction Accelerator
items.samenvatting_bron: Europe’s commitment to restore degraded ecosystems has created an urgent need to move from isolated restoration projects towards approaches that can be replicated and scaled. Wetland restoration, however, remains constrained by fragmented knowledge, incompatible datasets, inconsistent monitoring, limited transfer of experience between sites, weak stakeholder participation and insufficient links between ecological planning and long-term financing. Restore4Life addresses these barriers through an Integrated Wetland Reconstruction Accelerator that connects scientific evidence, digital decision support, field implementation, participation and finance throughout the restoration cycle. Within this framework, reconstruction refers to the active re-establishment of wetland structures, processes and functions where passive recovery alone is insufficient. The Accelerator provides a common operational framework for identifying restoration opportunities, establishing ecological baselines, selecting indicators, designing interventions, monitoring outcomes and comparing restoration trajectories. These approaches are being tested across contrasting freshwater, floodplain, deltaic and coastal demonstration sites and translated into harmonised protocols, transferable solutions and practical implementation roadmaps. items.samenvatting_bron: Aquatic invasive species disrupt ecosystem function and threaten native biodiversity through predation, competition, and habitat alteration. Eradication offers the best chance for ecosystem recovery but requires substantial time and resources, and detection of invasives at low densities is challenging. Environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling of genetic material shed by organisms into the environment provides a sensitive, cost-effective, and noninvasive alternative to traditional detection methods. In this study, we applied eDNA methods to inform invasive species eradication at Ash Meadows National Wildlife Refuge and explore spatiotemporal dynamics of endangered Ash Meadows Amargosa Pupfish (Cyprinodon nevadensis mionectes), and invasive Green Sunfish (Lepomis cyanellus), and Red Swamp Crayfish (Procambarus clarkii) in the target warm spring system. First, we quantified eDNA transport using a caged Green Sunfish experiment, then used these results to inform repeated eDNA sampling alongside traditional capture methods (gill nets, trap nets, electrofishing) to determine Green Sunfish distribution, target removal efforts, and evaluate eradication. Modeling indicated that collection of one sample every 160 m yielded >0.95 detection probability for 3 fish, while collection of 10 samples was required to reach the same detection probability for 1 fish (95% CI: 2–57). items.titel: Onderzoek naar een nieuwe, op DNA gebaseerde selectiemethode voor het identificeren van genclusters voor de biosynthese van antibiotica
items.samenvatting_bron: Antibiotics are indispensable for modern medicine as they allow the treatment of infectious diseases and enable invasive medical procedures. However, their incorrect and widespread use has caused an increase in antibiotic resistance, making the discovery of novel antibiotics urgent. Most antibiotics in clinical use are derived from micro-organisms. Unfortunately, traditional techniques suffer from the limited culturability and sensitivity needed to detect antibiotic-producing organisms, resulting in the discovery of only the "low hanging fruit" of antibiotic candidates. Accessing the large potential known to be still present in nature therefore requires new approaches to circumvent these limitations and expand the repertoire of antibiotics known today. In this work, we aimed to set the first steps towards a novel approach, using a polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based droplet-platform to adopt a genotype-based, culture-independent method with increased throughput and sensitivity. A PCR-assay with newly developed degenerate primers will be used to enrich gene cluster types of interest. Combined with high-throughput screening of large metagenomic libraries, built with environmental DNA (eDNA), and functional characterization of recovered clones, we anticipate that this approach will enable the detection of a larger diversity of antibiotics and complement current detection methodologies.

items.titel: Coastal benthic ecosystems in a changing ocean: a mini review
items.samenvatting_bron: Coastal benthic ecosystems are shaped by the combined effects of climate change and anthropogenic pressures. Ocean warming, acidification, and deoxygenation interact with eutrophication, pollution, bottom trawling, and coastal development, altering biodiversity, habitat structure, and functioning from shallow coasts to continental margins. Benthic communities, comprising infaunal and epifaunal taxa, regulate key processes including nutrient cycling, sediment dynamics, and carbon burial, thereby underpinning benthic-pelagic coupling and biogeochemical dynamics. Rising temperatures and marine heatwaves drive widespread losses of habitat-forming species, while ocean acidification constrains calcification. Warming, acidification, hypoxia, eutrophication, and pollution increasingly simplify assemblages, and alter trophic pathways and performance. Interactions among stressors can amplify organismal sensitivity and push ecosystems towards ecological thresholds. However, many knowledge gaps remain. Recent methodological advances, including environmental DNA metabarcoding, automated imaging, trait-based analyses, and multi-stressor experiments, are improving the detection of ecosystem changes at large and our mechanistic understanding of ecosystem responses to ongoing change. items.titel: Simple soil eDNA sampling reveals terrestrial mammal diversity in the Central Kalahari and highlights waterholes as sampling hotspots
items.samenvatting_bron: Remote and vast ecosystems present a challenge for biodiversity monitoring. The Central Kalahari Game Reserve in Botswana is one such ecosystem spanning 52,800 km2, a mosaic of fossilized rivers, clay pans, semi-arid sand dunes, scrub, and woodland. It is one of the last remaining untouched wildernesses in the world and hosts unique biodiversity, including populations of threatened mammals. Due to its extreme arid environment, size, and inaccessibility, surveying biodiversity across the reserve is both logistically and technically difficult. Here we demonstrate that a low-effort approach of sampling soil across the reserve is an efficient way to rapidly assess the terrestrial mammal biodiversity using eDNA metabarcoding. We found that eDNA from soil near waterholes performed better at capturing local biodiversity than soil from roads. eDNA metabarcoding detected 38 mammal species, 15 bird species and two amphibians and a simultaneously conducted camera trapping study detected 29 mammal species. eDNA was particularly powerful for detecting small-bodied taxa, including murids, mongooses and bats, which were largely missed by camera traps, while camera trapping was aimed at and performed well for detecting felids. Mammal species that had a higher activity nearby eDNA sampling points (i.e., a higher number of camera trapping recordings nearby) had a higher probability of being detected via eDNA. items.titel: Community-Driven Fisheries Innovations for Climate Adaptation and a Sustainable Blue Economy
items.samenvatting_bron: Abstract Small-scale fisheries are among the most climate-vulnerable socio-ecological systems, facing threats from rising sea temperatures, ocean acidification, extreme weather, and shifting species distributions. Yet, they are also dynamic sites of innovation where communities develop adaptive solutions. Drawing on a non-systematic review of literature from 2016–2025, this article synthesizes community-led innovations across Africa, Asia, Oceania, Europe, and Latin America and examines how local ecological knowledge, co-management, and technological practices converge to strengthen resilience. Across regions, empowerment emerges as both a mechanism and an outcome: women’s cooperatives in Nigeria and Mexico increased household security, youth-driven digital platforms in Ecuador and Hawaii built adaptive capacity, and Indigenous stewardship in North America safeguarded both biodiversity and cultural continuity. Scaling these innovations requires supportive governance, access to finance, and protections for local agencies. Far from being marginal, community-driven fisheries innovations are central to climate adaptation and must be recognized as core strategies for building a sustainable blue economy.

items.titel: Carbon Offsets 2.0
items.samenvatting_bron: Carbon offsetting was a well-intended but ill-fated model, ravaged by a lack of trust crisis stemming from methodological vices—additionality, permanence, and transparency—which has led to accusations of greenwashing and undermined the effectiveness of the entire procedure. This chapter suggests that a new paradigm, Carbon Offsets 2.0, is being formed, which is based on three non-negotiable pillars to reclaim integrity and impact. The first pillar, trust, is designed with the help of science-based standards such as the Core Carbon Principles and effective community involvement with the help of Free, Prior, and Informed Consent. The second is transparency which is a digital revolution of satellites monitoring, AI and blockchain to establish an unchangeable, open registry of all credits. The third pillar, Real Impact, will change the market dynamics associated with low-cost avoidance to high-durability carbon dioxide removal and initiatives that provide verifiable co-benefits. The chapter discusses the shifting implement tools of next-generation approaches, such as improved nature-based solutions or technological carbon removal and the new financing, including the advance market commitment, that can be used to support them.

items.titel: Traditional villages in the Nhue River Green Belt, Hanoi, Vietnam: a biophilic landscape framework for healthy and resilient urbanization
items.samenvatting_bron: Rapid urbanization and climate change are increasing pressure on traditional villages within Hanoi’s Nhue River Green Belt, where settlements, agricultural land, water systems, cultural heritage, and local livelihoods coexist within a strategic ecological buffer. While research on biophilic urbanism and healthy cities often focuses on parks, green–blue infrastructure, street greening, and building-scale design, less attention has been given to green-belt villages as socio-ecological landscape systems with potential health-supportive capacities. This paper develops a typology-based framework for ecological landscape organization supporting urban health. Drawing on policy review, field observation, spatial analysis, and secondary data, the study identifies key landscape assets and pressures, including water systems, productive and livelihood landscapes, cultural–social spaces, slow-mobility networks, and courtyard housing. Villages are differentiated by their relationship with water, spatial structure, and livelihood characteristics, and these assets are then translated into five health-related landscape capacities. The findings provide practical guidance for planning and policy by reframing green-belt villages as health-supportive ecological landscape infrastructure. items.titel: The EU, US, and China
items.samenvatting_bron: As the climate crisis intensifies, the scientific consensus is clear: reducing emissions alone is no longer sufficient. The large-scale removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is now a critical pillar for achieving global net-zero targets. This chapter examines the emerging global carbon removal economy, focusing on the divergent strategies, strengths, and weaknesses of the three primary economic and geopolitical actors: the European Union, the United States, and China. Moving beyond a simple technological comparison, it analyzes the interplay of policy, innovation, investment, and underlying philosophy that is shaping this nascent but vital industry. The chapter argues that while the US currently leads in market-creation and high-risk innovation, the EU excels in regulatory frameworks and methodological rigor, and China holds unparalleled potential for rapid deployment of nature-based solutions and industrial scale-up. The ultimate "leader" is not yet decided, and the evolving dynamics between these powers will fundamentally shape the cost, efficacy, and governance of carbon removal for decades to come.

items.titel: Biochar in Stabilizing Soil Organic Carbon and Building a Sustainable Bioeconomy
items.samenvatting_bron: Biochar appears to be a natural remedy that can enhance the stabilization of soil organic carbon (SOC). Biochar effectively enhances SOC stabilization and is increasingly recognized as a nature-based solution for developing sustainable bioeconomy pathways. This chapter discuss the soils in terms of their capacity to stabilize and store organic carbon. Soils serve as the ultimate carbon sink in terrestrial ecosystems. A high risk of SOC depletion has been reported in South Asian agroecosystems due to their intensive land use change, poor residue management, and climate-related stressors. According to recent studies, biochar has significant potential to replace depleted SOC with stable black carbon. The chapter also discusses the stabilization of SOC, its density and threat to degrade. This chapter provide essential insights for understanding the nature and dynamics of SOC pathways and mechanisms under dynamic soil conditions. The chapter also discusses important and critical aspects of biochar and black carbon along with their use in Indigenous soils, known as Terra preta.

The package includes derived analytic files, data dictionaries, source-data manifest, reproducibility scripts, direction and estimability audit outputs for ND-GAIN climate indicators, adjustment-set sensitivity analyses, two-way fixed-effects model outputs, robustness analyses, programme-plausibility check outputs, and manuscript-supporting materials. items.titel: Implementation of agricultural nutrient mitigation policies and nature-based solutions in Baltic and North Sea countries
items.samenvatting_bron: Nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) emissions from agricultural lands contribute to eutrophication and the degradation of surface waters. This paper studies the implementation of European agri-environmental policies to regulate these emissions in the North European coastal waters by promoting changes in agricultural practices through nutrient mitigation measures and nature-based solutions (NbS). By analyzing policy documents and results from co-creation, it compares the implementation of agricultural nutrient mitigation policies in four Baltic Sea countries—Denmark, Sweden, Finland, and Poland—as well as Norway, which borders the Atlantic and the North Sea. The findings suggest that water quality should be set as a priority in national implementation. Integrating NbS, ensuring stability and aligning agricultural practices with environmental goals would reduce the risk of eutrophication in marine ecosystems.

items.titel: IFAD Impact Assessment - Nepal (Federal Democratic Republic of) Adaptation for Smallholders in Hilly Areas Project (ASHA)
items.samenvatting_bron: The Adaptation for Smallholders in Hilly Areas Project (ASHA) was designed to enhance climate resilience among vulnerable smallholder farmers through a combination of grants, training, and capacity-building initiatives. Central to its approach was the strengthening of local climate adaptation planning via Local Adaptation Plans of Action (LAPAs) and the promotion of climate-smart agriculture through farmer field schools. The project also supported the development of climate-resilient communal infrastructure and encouraged climate-adaptive, income-generating activities, such as vegetable cultivation, agroforestry and livestock management, leveraging both financial and in-kind contributions from participating communities. This impact assessment of ASHA was conducted in 2023 using a mixed-methods approach that combines quantitative household and community-level surveys with qualitative interviews.

items.titel: Beyond Green Materials
items.samenvatting_bron: Abstract Climate adaptation governance in Pacific Small Island Developing States is increasingly influenced by market-oriented frameworks, including climate finance, private-sector partnerships, and resilience investment initiatives. While these approaches have expanded adaptation finance, they have also narrowed how resilience is understood and governed. They marginalize Indigenous systems of stewardship, customary governance, and community-led adaptation. This article examines bamboo-based adaptation in the district of Tai Vugalei, Fiji. It reframes bamboo not as a nature-based solution or green material but as Indigenous adaptive infrastructure rooted in custodianship, reciprocity, and community governance. Drawing on talanoa, a Pacific Indigenous approach to dialogue, storytelling, and knowledge sharing, alongside participant observation and lived Indigenous participation, the article shows how bamboo supports durable livelihoods and reparable infrastructure through communal learning, local governance, and practices that have endured over generations. The findings demonstrate how growing efforts to commercialize, standardize, and scale bamboo—how it is institutionalized, commercialized, and governed as it moves beyond village contexts—create tensions between community-based governance and market-oriented development pathways. items.titel: When does urban greening jointly mitigate urban heat and air pollution? A systematic evidence map of co-benefits, trade-offs and failure conditions
items.samenvatting_bron: Urban heat and air pollution are two major environmental challenges affecting urban sustainability, public health and quality of life. Urban green spaces, including parks, urban forests, street trees and other ground-level vegetation, are widely promoted as nature-based solutions to address these challenges. However, although vegetation can reduce temperatures through shading and evapotranspiration, its effects on air pollution are more complex. Dense vegetation may restrict airflow and pollutant dispersion, while some plant species release biogenic volatile organic compounds that contribute to atmospheric pollution. Consequently, improvements in thermal conditions do not necessarily lead to improvements in air quality. The primary purpose of this research is to systematically examine when and under what conditions urban greening provides simultaneous benefits for urban heat mitigation and air pollution reduction, when trade-offs occur, and which environmental and spatial factors influence these outcomes. The review also investigates whether improvements in environmental conditions translate into measurable reductions in human exposure or improvements in health and wellbeing. The research addresses five key questions: Under what conditions does urban greening improve both thermal conditions and air quality?
